claim: Human cells lacking delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin form abnormal centrioles characterized by an absence of triplet microtubules, lack of central core protein POC5, and a futile cycle of centriole formation and disintegration.
source: Previously, we found that human cells lacking delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin form abnormal centrioles, characterized by an absence of triplet microtubules, lack of central core protein POC5, and a futile cycle of centriole formation and disintegration (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Wang et al., 2017) and is consistent with data presented in the current manuscript.

claim: Human cells lacking either TEDC1 or TEDC2 have similar abnormalities to cells lacking delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin.
source: Here, we show that human cells lacking either TEDC1 or TEDC2 have similar abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 showing similar phenotypes across mutants.

claim: Mutant centrioles elongate to the same length as control centrioles in G2 phase.
source: Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we observed that mutant centrioles elongate to the same length as control centrioles in G2 phase and fail to recruit central core scaffold proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data presented in Figure 4A showing centriole lengths in different cell cycle phases.

claim: Mutant centrioles fail to recruit central core scaffold proteins.
source: Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we observed that mutant centrioles elongate to the same length as control centrioles in G2 phase and fail to recruit central core scaffold proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4E showing absence of POC5 and WDR90 in mutant centrioles.

claim: Mutant centrioles have an expanded proximal region.
source: Remarkably, mutant centrioles also have an expanded proximal region.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4F-I showing elongated localization of proximal end proteins SASS6, CEP135, STIL, and CPAP.

claim: During mitosis, mutant centrioles further elongate before fragmenting and disintegrating.
source: During mitosis, these mutant centrioles further elongate before fragmenting and disintegrating.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5 showing centriole elongation in prometaphase and fragmentation in later mitotic stages.

claim: TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 physically interact.
source: All four proteins physically interact and TEDC1 and TEDC2 can form a subcomplex in the absence of the tubulins, supporting an AlphaFold Multimer model of the tetramer.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3C and 3D showing physical interactions between the proteins.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 can form a subcomplex in the absence of the tubulins.
source: All four proteins physically interact and TEDC1 and TEDC2 can form a subcomplex in the absence of the tubulins, supporting an AlphaFold Multimer model of the tetramer.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown experiments in Figure 3C and 3D showing TEDC1-TEDC2 interaction in TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- cells.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 localize to centrosomes.
source: TEDC1 and TEDC2 localize to centrosomes and are mutually dependent on each other and on delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin for localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and U-ExM data in Figure 2 showing centrosomal localization of tagged TEDC1 and TEDC2.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 are mutually dependent on each other and on delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin for localization.
source: TEDC1 and TEDC2 localize to centrosomes and are mutually dependent on each other and on delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin for localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A and 3B showing loss of TEDC1 or TEDC2 centrosomal localization in various mutant backgrounds.

claim: Delta-tubulin, epsilon-tubulin, TEDC1, and TEDC2 function together to promote robust centriole architecture.
source: Our results demonstrate that delta-tubulin, epsilon-tubulin, TEDC1, and TEDC2 function together to promote robust centriole architecture, laying the foundation for future studies on the mechanisms underlying the assembly of triplet microtubules and their interactions with centriole structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective data showing similar phenotypes across all four mutants and their physical interactions.

claim: Centrioles have a unique, conserved architecture formed by three linked, 'triplet', microtubules arranged in ninefold symmetry.
source: Centrioles have a unique, conserved architecture formed by three linked, 'triplet', microtubules arranged in ninefold symmetry.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about centriole structure cited in the introduction.

claim: The centriole barrel walls are approximately 250 nm in diameter by 500 nm in length.
source: The unique architecture of the centriole is highly conserved: the centriole barrel walls of approximately 250 nm in diameter by 500 nm in length are formed of compound microtubules linked to each other through shared protofilament walls, arranged in ninefold symmetry (reviewed in Wang and Stearns, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article (Wang and Stearns, 2017).

claim: Centrioles exhibit proximal-distal polarity comprised of three subdomains: the proximal end with triplet microtubules, the distal end with doublet microtubules, and the central core spanning the two regions.
source: Centrioles exhibit proximal-distal polarity comprised of three subdomains: the proximal end with triplet microtubules, the distal end with doublet microtubules, and the central core spanning the two regions (LeGuennec et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to LeGuennec et al., 2021.

claim: The A-tubule is a complete microtubule formed of 13 protofilaments.
source: The A-tubule is a complete microtubule formed of 13 protofilaments, and the B- and C-tubules are partial tubules and share protofilament walls with adjacent tubules.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about centriole microtubule structure.

claim: The B- and C-tubules are partial tubules and share protofilament walls with adjacent tubules.
source: The A-tubule is a complete microtubule formed of 13 protofilaments, and the B- and C-tubules are partial tubules and share protofilament walls with adjacent tubules.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about centriole microtubule structure.

claim: Delta-tubulin (TUBD1) and epsilon-tubulin (TUBE1) are required for compound microtubule formation or stability in multiple organisms.
source: Two non-canonical members of the tubulin superfamily, delta-tubulin (TUBD1) and epsilon-tubulin (TUBE1), are required for compound microtubule formation or stability in multiple organisms (de Loubresse et al., 2001; Dupuis-Williams et al., 2002; Dutcher and Trabuco, 1998; Dutcher et al., 2002; Gadelha et al., 2006; Goodenough and StClair, 1975; Ross et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work across different organisms.

claim: Human cells lacking delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin make aberrant centrioles that only have singlet microtubules and disintegrate in mitosis.
source: Previously, we showed that human cells lacking these tubulins make aberrant centrioles that only have singlet microtubules and disintegrate in mitosis, resulting in a futile cycle of centriole formation and loss every cell cycle (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Wang et al., 2017).

claim: Mutant centrioles lacking delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin fail to recruit the distal end protein POC5.
source: These mutant centrioles fail to recruit the distal end protein POC5, indicating that compound microtubules may be required for centriole composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Wang et al., 2017) and data in the current manuscript.

claim: The cartwheel is a ninefold symmetric hub and spokes made from SASS6 and associated proteins.
source: At the proximal end, the cartwheel, a ninefold symmetric hub and spokes made from SASS6 and associated proteins, is connected to the A-tubule through the pinhead, which has been proposed to be formed of CEP135 and CPAP (Hatzopoulos et al., 2013; Kraatz et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2013a; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pinhead connects the cartwheel to the A-tubule and has been proposed to be formed of CEP135 and CPAP.
source: At the proximal end, the cartwheel, a ninefold symmetric hub and spokes made from SASS6 and associated proteins, is connected to the A-tubule through the pinhead, which has been proposed to be formed of CEP135 and CPAP (Hatzopoulos et al., 2013; Kraatz et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2013a; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents a proposed model.

claim: Multiple cartwheels are stacked within the centriole lumen to a height of approximately one-third of the entire centriole length (~170 nm in human centrioles).
source: Multiple cartwheels are stacked within the centriole lumen to a height of approximately one-third of the entire centriole length (~170 nm in human centrioles; Klena et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Klena et al., 2020.

claim: CCDC77, WDR67, and MIIP were identified to be components of the A-C linkers.
source: Recently CCDC77, WDR67, and MIIP were identified to be components of the A-C linkers (Bournonville et al., 2024; Laporte et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: A helical inner scaffold within the central core imparts structural integrity upon the centriole.
source: Within the central core, a helical inner scaffold imparts structural integrity upon the centriole (Le Guennec et al., 2020; Steib et al., 2020), and recruits proteins, including gamma-tubulin, to the lumen of the centriole (Schweizer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The helical inner scaffold is composed of POC5, POC1B, FAM161A, WDR90, and CCDC15.
source: This scaffold is formed in G2-phase of the first cell cycle after centriole birth, is composed of POC5, POC1B, FAM161A, WDR90, and CCDC15 and contacts all three (A-, B-, and C-) tubules of the triplet (Arslanhan et al., 2023; Laporte et al., 2024; Le Guennec et al., 2020; Steib et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The helical inner scaffold is formed in G2-phase of the first cell cycle after centriole birth.
source: This scaffold is formed in G2-phase of the first cell cycle after centriole birth, is composed of POC5, POC1B, FAM161A, WDR90, and CCDC15 and contacts all three (A-, B-, and C-) tubules of the triplet (Arslanhan et al., 2023; Laporte et al., 2024; Le Guennec et al., 2020; Steib et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The helical inner scaffold contacts all three (A-, B-, and C-) tubules of the triplet.
source: This scaffold is formed in G2-phase of the first cell cycle after centriole birth, is composed of POC5, POC1B, FAM161A, WDR90, and CCDC15 and contacts all three (A-, B-, and C-) tubules of the triplet (Arslanhan et al., 2023; Laporte et al., 2024; Le Guennec et al., 2020; Steib et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The distal region of centrioles has a unique protein composition, including centrin, CP110, SFI1, CEP97, CEP90, OFD1, and MNR.
source: The distal region of centrioles also has a unique protein composition, including the proteins centrin, CP110, SFI1, CEP97, CEP90, OFD1, and MNR (Kleylein-Sohn et al., 2007; Kumar et al., 2021; Laporte et al., 2022; Laporte et al., 2024; Le Borgne et al., 2022; Spektor et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In cycling cells, one newly formed procentriole is created at the proximal end of each pre-existing parental centriole in S-phase, resulting in four centrioles within the cell.
source: Canonically, centriole formation in cycling cells is 'templated', in which one newly formed procentriole is created at the proximal end of each pre-existing parental centriole in S-phase, resulting in four centrioles within the cell.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about centriole duplication.

claim: During the first cycle after their formation, procentrioles acquire post-translational modifications, elongate, recruit the inner scaffold, lose the cartwheel, and undergo centriole-to-centrosome conversion.
source: During the first cycle after their formation, procentrioles acquire post-translational modifications, elongate, recruit the inner scaffold, lose the cartwheel, and undergo centriole-to-centrosome conversion.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about centriole maturation.

claim: Additional changes occur during the second cell cycle, including acquisition of the distal and subdistal appendages that are important for ciliogenesis.
source: Additional changes occur during the second cell cycle, including acquisition of the distal and subdistal appendages that are important for ciliogenesis (Sullenberger et al., 2020; Tischer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When parental centrioles are ablated, centrioles can form de novo in S-phase.
source: Under experimental manipulations in which the parental centrioles are ablated, centrioles can also form de novo in S-phase (Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wong et al., 2015.

claim: De novo centriole formation can result in more than five centrioles per cell and has been shown to be error-prone.
source: De novo centriole formation can result in more than five centrioles per cell and has been shown to be error-prone (Wang et al., 2015), perhaps indicating differences in centriole structure or regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015 and includes speculation about the implications.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 physically interact with TUBD1 and TUBE1.
source: These proteins physically interact with TUBD1 and TUBE1 (Breslow et al., 2018; Huttlin et al., 2017; Huttlin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of Tedc1 or Tedc2 in 3T3 cells results in a variable distribution of centriole numbers through the cell cycle.
source: Loss of Tedc1 or Tedc2 in 3T3 cells results in a variable distribution of centriole numbers through the cell cycle, and tagged TEDC1 localizes to centrosomes (Breslow et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Breslow et al., 2018.

claim: Tagged TEDC1 localizes to centrosomes in 3T3 cells.
source: Loss of Tedc1 or Tedc2 in 3T3 cells results in a variable distribution of centriole numbers through the cell cycle, and tagged TEDC1 localizes to centrosomes (Breslow et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Breslow et al., 2018.

claim: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells were created in the same background as the TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutants (hTERT RPE-1 TP53-/-).
source: We created TEDC1-/- or TEDC2-/- mutant cells in the same background as the TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutants and found that these cells phenocopy loss of TUBD1 or TUBE1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- cells phenocopy loss of TUBD1 or TUBE1.
source: We created TEDC1-/- or TEDC2-/- mutant cells in the same background as the TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutants and found that these cells phenocopy loss of TUBD1 or TUBE1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1 showing similar phenotypes.

claim: Compound microtubules are required for recruiting the helical inner scaffold.
source: We find that the compound microtubules are required for recruiting the helical inner scaffold and correctly positioning the proximal end.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4E showing absence of inner scaffold proteins in mutant centrioles.

claim: Compound microtubules are required for correctly positioning the proximal end.
source: We find that the compound microtubules are required for recruiting the helical inner scaffold and correctly positioning the proximal end.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4F-I showing elongated proximal end in mutant centrioles.

claim: Centrioles formed de novo are very similar to procentrioles formed by templated centriole duplication in composition and architecture.
source: As part of our analysis, we also determine the composition and architecture of centrioles formed de novo and find that these are very similar to those of procentrioles formed by templated centriole duplication.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data in Figure 4 showing similar protein localization patterns.

claim: Compound microtubules are required for scaffolding substructures within centrioles and maintaining centriole stability through the cell cycle.
source: Together, these results indicate that compound microtubules are required for scaffolding substructures within centrioles and maintaining centriole stability through the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the collective data showing loss of inner scaffold and centriole disintegration in mutants.

claim: About half of TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells in asynchronous culture had no centrioles, and half had five or more centrioles.
source: By immunofluorescence staining for two centriolar proteins, centrin (CETN) and CP110, we observed that TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells had similar phenotypes to each other and to TUBD1-/- and TUBE1-/- mutant cells: in an asynchronously growing culture, about half of the cells had no centrioles, and half had five or more centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B showing centriole number distributions.

claim: The phenotypes of TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- cells were fully rescued by expression of tagged TEDC1 or TEDC2.
source: These phenotypes were fully rescued by expression of tagged TEDC1 (TEDC1-Halotag-3xFlag) or TEDC2 (TEDC2-V5-APEX2; Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1 showing rescue of centriole phenotypes.

claim: Almost all TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells lacked centrioles in G0/G1 phase.
source: We synchronized cells in each stage of the cell cycle, quantified the number of cells with centrioles, and found that almost all mutant cells lacked centrioles in G0/G1 phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B showing centriole numbers in synchronized cells.

claim: Centrioles formed in S-phase in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells and disintegrated in M.
source: Centrioles formed in S-phase and disintegrated in M (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B showing centriole numbers across cell cycle stages.

claim: All centrioles in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells were positive for the procentriole marker SASS6.
source: The centrioles that were present in mutant cells were immature: all centrioles were positive for the procentriole marker SASS6 and negative for the mature centriole marker CEP164 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1C showing SASS6 staining.

claim: All centrioles in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells were negative for the mature centriole marker CEP164.
source: The centrioles that were present in mutant cells were immature: all centrioles were positive for the procentriole marker SASS6 and negative for the mature centriole marker CEP164 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1D showing absence of CEP164 staining.

claim: Centrioles in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells lacked compound microtubules and only had singlet microtubules.
source: Similar to cells lacking delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin, we found that centrioles in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant cells lacked compound microtubules and only had singlet microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data in Figure 1E and F.

claim: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant centrioles had cartwheels and pinheads.
source: These centrioles had cartwheels and pinheads, but A-C linkers were not visible (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data in Figure 1E and F.

claim: A-C linkers were not visible in TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant centrioles.
source: These centrioles had cartwheels and pinheads, but A-C linkers were not visible (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data in Figure 1E and F.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 are expressed at low levels in cells.
source: TEDC1 and TEDC2 are expressed at low levels in cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and we could not reproducibly localize the endogenous proteins with antibody staining.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Tagged TEDC1 and TEDC2 rescue constructs localize to centrosomes.
source: We found that the tagged rescue constructs localize to centrosomes (Figure 2A and B) and the antibodies for the tags were specific (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A and B.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 were enriched at centrosomes in S/G2 and colocalized with SASS6, but not centrin.
source: TEDC1 and TEDC2 were enriched at centrosomes in S/G2 and colocalized with SASS6, but not centrin, indicating that TEDC1 and TEDC2 may localize to newly formed procentrioles and/or the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A and B showing colocalization patterns.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 may localize to newly formed procentrioles and/or the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
source: TEDC1 and TEDC2 were enriched at centrosomes in S/G2 and colocalized with SASS6, but not centrin, indicating that TEDC1 and TEDC2 may localize to newly formed procentrioles and/or the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the colocalization patterns observed in Figure 2.

claim: Both TEDC1 and TEDC2 localize to procentrioles and the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
source: With all three methods, we observed that both proteins localize to procentrioles and the proximal ends of parental centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple imaging methods shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 overlap with the centriolar microtubules at procentrioles and proximal ends of parental centrioles.
source: At these regions, both proteins overlap with the centriolar microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 2C and D showing overlap with acetylated tubulin.

claim: TEDC1 did not localize to centrioles in the absence of TEDC2, TUBD1, or TUBE1.
source: We found that TEDC1 did not localize to centrioles in the absence of TEDC2, TUBD1, or TUBE1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A.

claim: TEDC2 did not localize to centrioles in the absence of TEDC1, TUBD1, or TUBE1.
source: Likewise, TEDC2 did not localize to centrioles in the absence of TEDC1, TUBD1, or TUBE1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B.

claim: Overexpression of TEDC1 or TEDC2 did not rescue the centriole phenotypes in any of the other mutants.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of TEDC1 or TEDC2 did not rescue the centriole phenotypes in any of the other mutants, indicating that TEDC1 and TEDC2 are not downstream effectors of TUBD1 and TUBE1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3A and B showing lack of rescue.

claim: TEDC1 and TEDC2 are not downstream effectors of TUBD1 and TUBE1.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of TEDC1 or TEDC2 did not rescue the centriole phenotypes in any of the other mutants, indicating that TEDC1 and TEDC2 are not downstream effectors of TUBD1 and TUBE1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the lack of rescue observed in Figure 3A and B.

claim: TEDC1 did not interact with epsilon-tubulin in the absence of delta-tubulin.
source: TEDC1 did not interact with epsilon-tubulin in the absence of delta-tubulin, nor did it interact with delta-tubulin in the absence of TUBE1.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C.

claim: TEDC1 did not interact with delta-tubulin in the absence of TUBE1.
source: TEDC1 did not interact with epsilon-tubulin in the absence of delta-tubulin, nor did it interact with delta-tubulin in the absence of TUBE1.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of TEDC2, TEDC1 did not interact with TUBD1 or TUBE1.
source: In the absence of TEDC2, TEDC1 did not interact with TUBD1 or TUBE1.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of TUBD1 or TUBE1, TEDC1 and TEDC2 could still interact with each other.
source: However, in the absence of TUBD1 or TUBE1, TEDC1 and TEDC2 could still interact with each other (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3C.

claim: TEDC2 did not interact with either tubulin in the absence of the other.
source: TEDC2 did not interact with either tubulin in the absence of the other.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3D.

claim: In the absence of TEDC1, TEDC2 did not interact with either tubulin.
source: In the absence of TEDC1, TEDC2 did not interact with either tubulin.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data in Figure 3D.

claim: AlphaFold-Multimer predicted that TUBD1 and TUBE1 would form a heterodimer, similar to the alpha-tubulin/beta-tubulin heterodimer, with TUBD1 at the minus-end of the heterodimer.
source: AlphaFold-Multimer predicted that TUBD1 and TUBE1 would form a heterodimer, similar to the alpha-tubulin/beta-tubulin heterodimer, with TUBD1 at the minus-end of the heterodimer.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 3E.

claim: AlphaFold predicted that the alpha-helices of TEDC1 and TEDC2 interact with each other.
source: AlphaFold also predicted that the alpha-helices of TEDC1 and TEDC2 interact with each other, and that TEDC1 and TEDC2 form an interaction surface with TUBD1.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 3E.

claim: AlphaFold predicted that TEDC1 and TEDC2 form an interaction surface with TUBD1.
source: AlphaFold also predicted that the alpha-helices of TEDC1 and TEDC2 interact with each other, and that TEDC1 and TEDC2 form an interaction surface with TUBD1.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The AlphaFold predictions at the interface between TEDC1, TEDC2, and TUBD1 yielded high confidence pLDDT and PAE scores.
source: These predictions, especially at the interface between TEDC1, TEDC2, and TUBD1, yielded high confidence pLDDT and PAE scores (Figure 3E-G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational predictions shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: AlphaFold-Multimer did not predict a high-confidence interaction for TEDC1, TEDC2, alpha- and beta-tubulin.
source: While AlphaFold-Multimer did not predict a high-confidence interaction for TEDC1, TEDC2, alpha- and beta-tubulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), it did predict a high-confidence structure for Xenopus TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1, similar to that predicted for the human proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AlphaFold-Multimer predicted a high-confidence structure for Xenopus TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1, similar to that predicted for the human proteins.
source: While AlphaFold-Multimer did not predict a high-confidence interaction for TEDC1, TEDC2, alpha- and beta-tubulin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), it did predict a high-confidence structure for Xenopus TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1, similar to that predicted for the human proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Antibodies against acetylated alpha-tubulin stained mutant centrioles well.
source: We found that antibodies against acetylated alpha-tubulin stained mutant centrioles well (Figure 4B), indicating that centrioles with only singlet A-tubules can be acetylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4B.

claim: Centrioles with only singlet A-tubules can be acetylated.
source: We found that antibodies against acetylated alpha-tubulin stained mutant centrioles well (Figure 4B), indicating that centrioles with only singlet A-tubules can be acetylated.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the acetylated tubulin staining in Figure 4B.

claim: In S-phase, centrioles were short in all conditions.
source: In S-phase, centrioles were short in all conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by length measurements in Figure 4A.

claim: In G2-phase, centrioles elongated in all conditions, and mutant centrioles reached approximately similar lengths as control centrioles.
source: In G2-phase, centrioles elongated in all conditions, and mutant centrioles reached approximately similar lengths as control centrioles (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by length measurements in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutant centriole widths did not increase and centrioles remained narrow.
source: By contrast, mutant centriole widths did not increase and centrioles remained narrow, as we previously reported (Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by width measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and citation to prior work.

claim: CEP120 was present and properly localized within mutant centrioles.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, CEP120, a protein involved in regulating centriole length (Comartin et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013b; Mahjoub et al., 2010), was present and properly localized within mutant centrioles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mutant and control centrioles could be stained by GT335 antibody.
source: We found that mutant and control centrioles could be stained by GT335 (Figure 4C), indicating that mutant centrioles are at least mono-glutamylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutant centrioles are at least mono-glutamylated.
source: We found that mutant and control centrioles could be stained by GT335 (Figure 4C), indicating that mutant centrioles are at least mono-glutamylated.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on GT335 staining in Figure 4C.

claim: The polyE antibody did not label control procentrioles or de novo centrioles in the first cell cycle after their formation.
source: However, the polyE antibody did not label control procentrioles or de novo centrioles in the first cell cycle after their formation, making this antibody uninformative for our mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4D.

claim: Centriole glutamylation is a multi-step process, in which long glutamate side chains are added later during centriole maturation.
source: These results show that centrioles with just singlet microtubules (A-tubules) can be mono-glutamylated. Moreover, similar to previous reports (Sullenberger et al., 2020), our results suggest that centriole glutamylation is a multi-step process, in which long glutamate side chains are added later during centriole maturation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differential staining with GT335 and polyE antibodies, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant centrioles failed to recruit POC5.
source: Using expansion microscopy, we found that TEDC1-/- and TEDC2-/- mutant centrioles also failed to recruit POC5 (Figure 4Ei).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4Ei.

claim: The helical inner scaffold is not properly formed in centrioles with singlet microtubules.
source: Since our original work was published, POC5 was shown to be a component of the helical inner scaffold within the central core. These results indicate that the helical inner scaffold is not properly formed in centrioles with singlet microtubules.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of POC5 in mutant centrioles shown in Figure 4Ei.

claim: WDR90 was not recruited to mutant centrioles.
source: We found that WDR90 was not recruited to mutant centrioles, in contrast to control centrioles, in which it is recruited in G2-phase (Figure 4Eii).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4Eii.

claim: Mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules fail to build or stabilize the inner junction between the A- and B-tubules.
source: From these results, it is likely that mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules fail to build or stabilize the inner junction between the A- and B-tubules.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of WDR90 in mutant centrioles.

claim: In the absence of the inner junction and junctional protein WDR90, centrioles with singlet microtubules cannot form the inner scaffold.
source: In the absence of the inner junction and junctional protein WDR90, centrioles with singlet microtubules cannot form the inner scaffold.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of both WDR90 and POC5 in mutant centrioles.

claim: Gamma-tubulin was not detected within the lumen of control or de novo-formed centrioles in S or G2-phase.
source: As also previously reported (Laporte et al., 2024), we failed to detect gamma-tubulin within the lumen of control or de novo-formed centrioles in S or G2-phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and thus were unable to test whether gamma-tubulin, which is recruited to the lumen of centrioles by the inner scaffold, was mislocalized in mutant centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and citation to prior work.

claim: SASS6 was present within the lumen of control and mutant centrioles in S-phase.
source: We found that the centriolar cartwheel protein, SASS6, was present within the lumen of control and mutant centrioles in S-phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4F.

claim: In control centrioles in G2-phase, SASS6 was restricted to just the proximal end.
source: In control centrioles in G2-phase, SASS6 was restricted to just the proximal end.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4F.

claim: SASS6 was elongated in all G2-phase mutant centrioles.
source: Surprisingly, SASS6 was elongated in all G2-phase mutant centrioles (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: CEP135, STIL, CPAP, and CEP44 showed elongated localization in mutant centrioles similar to SASS6.
source: We observed a similar phenotype with multiple other proximal-end proteins: CEP135, STIL, CPAP, and CEP44 (Figure 4G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that the entire proximal end is elongated in mutant centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4G-I and supplementary figures.

claim: The entire proximal end is elongated in mutant centrioles.
source: We observed a similar phenotype with multiple other proximal-end proteins: CEP135, STIL, CPAP, and CEP44 (Figure 4G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that the entire proximal end is elongated in mutant centrioles.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the elongated localization of multiple proximal end proteins.

claim: The extended localization of proximal end proteins was not due to increased protein expression in mutant cells.
source: The extended localization of proximal end proteins was not due to increased protein expression in mutant cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: CETN2 and CP110 were localized to mutant centrioles and clearly marked one end of the centriole barrel in both S-phase and G2-phase.
source: We found that CETN2 and CP110, two proteins of the distal centriole, were localized to mutant centrioles and clearly marked one end of the centriole barrel in both S-phase and G2-phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Proximal-to-distal centriole polarity was unaffected in mutant centrioles.
source: We conclude that proximal-to-distal centriole polarity was unaffected in mutant centrioles, and proximal end elongation did not affect the recruitment of proteins to the centriole distal end.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the proper localization of distal end proteins in mutant centrioles.

claim: Proximal end elongation did not affect the recruitment of proteins to the centriole distal end.
source: We conclude that proximal-to-distal centriole polarity was unaffected in mutant centrioles, and proximal end elongation did not affect the recruitment of proteins to the centriole distal end.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the proper localization of distal end proteins despite proximal end elongation.

claim: Centrioles lacking compound microtubules are unable to properly regulate the length of the proximal end.
source: Together, these results indicate that centrioles lacking compound microtubules are unable to properly regulate the length of the proximal end.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the elongated proximal end observed in mutant centrioles.

claim: CEP295 was present and normally localized within mutant centrioles in both S- and G2-phases.
source: Using U-ExM, we found that CEP295 was present and normally localized within mutant centrioles in both S- and G2-phases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Centriole loss in mutants is unlikely to be due to loss of CEP295 localization.
source: We conclude that centriole loss in our mutants is unlikely to be due to loss of CEP295 localization, and therefore that TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 are likely part of a different pathway required for centriole stability through the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the normal CEP295 localization in mutant centrioles.

claim: TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 are likely part of a different pathway required for centriole stability through the cell cycle.
source: We conclude that centriole loss in our mutants is unlikely to be due to loss of CEP295 localization, and therefore that TEDC1, TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1 are likely part of a different pathway required for centriole stability through the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the normal CEP295 localization despite centriole loss.

claim: In prometaphase stage TUBD1-/- or TUBE1-/- cells, centrioles were longer than normal, with an elongated proximal end marked by SASS6, and a CP110-positive cap.
source: By contrast, in prometaphase stage TUBD1-/- or TUBE1-/- cells, we found that centrioles had a unique appearance: they were longer than normal, with an elongated proximal end marked by SASS6, and a CP110-positive cap.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5C and E.

claim: The two ends of prometaphase mutant centrioles were connected by weak monoE staining.
source: These two ends were connected by weak monoE staining (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5C and E.

claim: After metaphase, centrioles in mutant cells were either completely absent, or had a fragmented appearance.
source: After metaphase, centrioles in mutant cells were either completely absent, or had a fragmented appearance (Figure 5D and F), with aggregates of staining that did not resemble true centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5D and F.

claim: In mutant cells, centrioles elongate in early mitosis to form an aberrant intermediate structure, followed by fragmentation in late mitosis.
source: We conclude that in our mutant cells, centrioles elongate in early mitosis to form an aberrant intermediate structure, followed by fragmentation in late mitosis.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the progression of centriole changes observed in Figure 5.

claim: The absence of the inner scaffold arises from the loss of the B- and C-tubules within centrioles.
source: We propose that the absence of the inner scaffold arises from the loss of the B- and C-tubules within centrioles, which may serve to anchor WDR90 and/or other proteins of the inner scaffold.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing absence of inner scaffold in mutant centrioles.

claim: The B- and C-tubules may serve to anchor WDR90 and/or other proteins of the inner scaffold.
source: We propose that the absence of the inner scaffold arises from the loss of the B- and C-tubules within centrioles, which may serve to anchor WDR90 and/or other proteins of the inner scaffold.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: WDR90 has been proposed to localize to the inner junction between the A- and B-tubules and is required for recruiting other inner scaffold components.
source: WDR90 has been proposed to localize to the inner junction between the A- and B-tubules and is required for recruiting other inner scaffold components (Le Guennec et al., 2020; Steib et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The B-tubule is required to recruit or stabilize WDR90 at the inner junction.
source: We find that mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules fail to localize WDR90, and thus speculate that the B-tubule is required to recruit or stabilize WDR90 at the inner junction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the absence of WDR90 in mutant centrioles lacking B-tubules.

claim: The inner scaffold makes connections to all three (A-, B-, and C-) tubules by cryo-electron tomography.
source: In addition, by cryo-electron tomography, the inner scaffold makes connections to all three (A-, B-, and C-) tubules.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: Mutant centrioles with only A-tubules may fail to provide anchoring sites for other proteins within the inner scaffold.
source: Although the identities of all the proteins that form these connections have not been determined, it is possible that mutant centrioles with only A-tubules also fail to provide anchoring sites for the other proteins within the inner scaffold.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural requirements of the inner scaffold.

claim: The compound microtubules of centrioles are required for proper formation of the inner helical scaffold of the central core.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the compound microtubules of centrioles are required for proper formation of the inner helical scaffold of the central core.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the absence of inner scaffold in mutant centrioles lacking compound microtubules.

claim: The triplet microtubules, the inner scaffold, and/or the TUBD1/TUBE1/TEDC1/TEDC2 protein complex might act to limit the length of the proximal end.
source: It is possible that the triplet microtubules, the inner scaffold, and/or the TUBD1/TUBE1/TEDC1/TEDC2 protein complex might act to limit the length of the proximal end.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms regulating proximal end length.

claim: Loss of the inner scaffold protein POC1A results in centrioles with extended regions of some proximal proteins, including CEP44, CEP135, and CEP295.
source: Recently, loss of the inner scaffold protein POC1A has been shown to result in centrioles with extended regions of some proximal proteins, including CEP44, CEP135, and CEP295, indicating that the inner scaffold regulates the extent of these proteins (Sala et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sala et al., 2024.

claim: The inner scaffold regulates the extent of proximal proteins CEP44, CEP135, and CEP295.
source: Recently, loss of the inner scaffold protein POC1A has been shown to result in centrioles with extended regions of some proximal proteins, including CEP44, CEP135, and CEP295, indicating that the inner scaffold regulates the extent of these proteins (Sala et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the cited work.

claim: POC1A-/- mutant centrioles can form triplet microtubules and do not have extended SASS6 staining.
source: Interestingly, unlike our mutant centrioles which have singlet microtubules, POC1A-/- mutant centrioles can form triplet microtubules and do not have extended SASS6 staining (Sala et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sala et al., 2024.

claim: The height of the cartwheel may be regulated by the triplet microtubules.
source: This suggests that the height of the cartwheel may be regulated by the triplet microtubules.
evidence: This is speculation based on the comparison with POC1A-/- centrioles.

claim: The cartwheel and centriolar microtubules have been proposed to assemble interdependently to impart ninefold symmetry upon the centriole.
source: The cartwheel and centriolar microtubules have been proposed to assemble interdependently to impart ninefold symmetry upon the centriole (Hilbert et al., 2016), and it is possible that interdependent assembly also regulates the height of the cartwheel.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hilbert et al., 2016 and includes speculation.

claim: Interdependent assembly of cartwheel and centriolar microtubules may also regulate the height of the cartwheel.
source: The cartwheel and centriolar microtubules have been proposed to assemble interdependently to impart ninefold symmetry upon the centriole (Hilbert et al., 2016), and it is possible that interdependent assembly also regulates the height of the cartwheel.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed interdependent assembly.

claim: Many aspects of centriole architecture are unaffected in mutant centrioles, including formation of the distal tip, centriole length regulation prior to mitosis, acquisition of post-translational modifications, establishment of proximal-distal polarity, and recruitment of proteins required for centriole-to-centrosome conversion.
source: Many aspects of centriole architecture, including formation of the distal tip, centriole length regulation prior to mitosis, acquisition of post-translational modifications, establishment of proximal-distal polarity, and recruitment of proteins required for centriole-to-centrosome conversion, are unaffected in mutant centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by data throughout Figure 4 showing normal localization of various proteins.

claim: The proteins that regulate centriole architecture aspects can act upon the A-tubule independently of the B- and C-tubules.
source: These results indicate that the proteins that regulate these processes can act upon the A-tubule independently of the B- and C-tubules.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the normal localization of many proteins in mutant centrioles with only A-tubules.

claim: Mammalian cells engineered to lack CEP295 form centrioles that are lost through the cell cycle, due to an inability to undergo centriole to centrosome conversion.
source: Centriole loss is not unique to centrioles lacking compound microtubules: mammalian cells engineered to lack CEP295 also form centrioles that are lost through the cell cycle, due to an inability to undergo centriole to centrosome conversion (Izquierdo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Izquierdo et al., 2014.

claim: In Drosophila oocytes, down-regulation of Polo kinase and pericentriolar material triggers centriole elimination.
source: Similarly, in Drosophila oocytes, down-regulation of Polo kinase and pericentriolar material triggers centriole elimination (Pimenta-Marques et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pimenta-Marques et al., 2016.

claim: Centriole loss in mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules may be independent of centriole to centrosome conversion and pericentriolar material recruitment.
source: We find that CEP295 is properly localized in mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules, indicating that centriole loss in this context may be independent of centriole to centrosome conversion and pericentriolar material recruitment.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the normal CEP295 localization in mutant centrioles.

claim: Centriole loss is correlated with loss of the SASS6 cartwheel in mitosis.
source: Using expansion microscopy, we find that centriole loss is correlated with loss of the SASS6 cartwheel in mitosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by U-ExM data in Figure 5 showing SASS6 loss in anaphase.

claim: Mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules resemble centriole loss within C. elegans oocytes, in which the central tube is lost prior to centriole widening and subsequent loss of the centriolar microtubules.
source: In this regard, mutant centrioles with singlet microtubules resemble centriole loss within C. elegans oocytes, in which an analogous structure to the cartwheel named the central tube is lost prior to centriole widening and subsequent loss of the centriolar microtubules (Pierron et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is a comparison to prior work supported by citation to Pierron et al., 2023.

claim: Prolonged mitotic arrest has been reported to result in centriole over elongation through Plk1 activity.
source: Prolonged mitotic arrest has been reported to result in centriole over elongation through Plk1 activity (Kong et al., 2020), and it is possible that a lengthened mitosis, as observed in these mutant cells and cells lacking centrioles (Farrell et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2017), may also result in over elongation of mutant centrioles with just A-tubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kong et al., 2020.

claim: A lengthened mitosis may result in over elongation of mutant centrioles with just A-tubules.
source: Prolonged mitotic arrest has been reported to result in centriole over elongation through Plk1 activity (Kong et al., 2020), and it is possible that a lengthened mitosis, as observed in these mutant cells and cells lacking centrioles (Farrell et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2017), may also result in over elongation of mutant centrioles with just A-tubules.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited work and observations in mutant cells.

claim: CPAP has an expanded domain in mutant centrioles compared to controls.
source: In addition, we note that CPAP has an expanded domain in mutant centrioles compared to controls (Figure 4, Vásquez-Limeta et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4 and citation to prior work.

claim: CPAP is involved in slow processive microtubule growth.
source: CPAP is involved in slow processive microtubule growth (Sharma et al., 2016) and its loss results in centriole fragmentation (Vásquez-Limeta et al., 2022), and it is possible that CPAP mislocalization may also contribute to over elongation of these mutant centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sharma et al., 2016.

claim: Loss of CPAP results in centriole fragmentation.
source: CPAP is involved in slow processive microtubule growth (Sharma et al., 2016) and its loss results in centriole fragmentation (Vásquez-Limeta et al., 2022), and it is possible that CPAP mislocalization may also contribute to over elongation of these mutant centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vásquez-Limeta et al., 2022.

claim: CPAP mislocalization may contribute to over elongation of mutant centrioles.
source: CPAP is involved in slow processive microtubule growth (Sharma et al., 2016) and its loss results in centriole fragmentation (Vásquez-Limeta et al., 2022), and it is possible that CPAP mislocalization may also contribute to over elongation of these mutant centrioles.
evidence: This is speculation based on the expanded CPAP domain and its known functions.

claim: Mutant human centrioles lacking compound microtubules bear similarities to the centrioles of Drosophila and C. elegans embryos.
source: Finally, we note that mutant human centrioles lacking compound microtubules bear similarities to the centrioles of Drosophila and C. elegans embryos, which have evolved to lack triplet microtubules and have cartwheels extending the entire length of the centriole (González et al., 1998; Pelletier et al., 2006; Woglar et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is a comparison to prior work supported by citations.

claim: Drosophila and C. elegans embryos have evolved to lack triplet microtubules and have cartwheels extending the entire length of the centriole.
source: Finally, we note that mutant human centrioles lacking compound microtubules bear similarities to the centrioles of Drosophila and C. elegans embryos, which have evolved to lack triplet microtubules and have cartwheels extending the entire length of the centriole (González et al., 1998; Pelletier et al., 2006; Woglar et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Embryonic centrioles in Drosophila and C. elegans are shorter than that of other organisms.
source: Embryonic centrioles in both species are shorter than that of other organisms, and helical inner scaffolds have not been reported.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Helical inner scaffolds have not been reported in Drosophila and C. elegans embryonic centrioles.
source: Embryonic centrioles in both species are shorter than that of other organisms, and helical inner scaffolds have not been reported.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Embryonic centrioles in Drosophila and C. elegans participate in mitosis, can duplicate their centrioles, and serve as basal bodies for sensory cilia.
source: In both species, these diminished centrioles participate in mitosis, can duplicate their centrioles, and serve as basal bodies for sensory cilia.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about centriole function in these organisms.

claim: Centrioles with triplet microtubules and the proteins they anchor, including the inner scaffold, may be required for centriole function in organisms with motile cilia.
source: We speculate that centrioles with triplet microtubules and the proteins they anchor, including the inner scaffold, may be required for centriole function in organisms with motile cilia, perhaps to help stabilize the basal body against ciliary movement.
evidence: This is speculation based on the comparison with organisms lacking triplet microtubules.

claim: Triplet microtubules may help stabilize the basal body against ciliary movement.
source: We speculate that centrioles with triplet microtubules and the proteins they anchor, including the inner scaffold, may be required for centriole function in organisms with motile cilia, perhaps to help stabilize the basal body against ciliary movement.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of triplet microtubules.

claim: Mutating an inner scaffold protein, Poc1, in Tetrahymena results in abnormal bending within basal bodies.
source: Such activity has been described for Tetrahymena basal bodies, and mutating an inner scaffold protein, Poc1, results in abnormal bending within basal bodies (Junker et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Junker et al., 2022.

claim: Drosophila spermatocytes have basal bodies with triplet microtubules.
source: Further supporting this hypothesis, Drosophila spermatocytes, one of the few cells within this species with motile cilia, have basal bodies with triplet microtubules (González et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to González et al., 1998.

claim: Drosophila spermatocytes likely form triplet microtubules in an alternative manner, as Drosophila lacks delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin.
source: We note that these spermatocytes likely form triplet microtubules in an alternative manner, as Drosophila lacks delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of triplet microtubules in Drosophila spermatocytes despite lacking delta- and epsilon-tubulin.

claim: The AlphaFold-Multimer predicted tetrameric complex would be approximately 13 nm in length and 6 nm in width.
source: Our AlphaFold models indicate that such a structure would be approximately 13 nm in length and 6 nm in width.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from the AlphaFold-Multimer prediction shown in Figure 3E.

claim: It is possible that the tetrameric complex helps form the A-C linker, the pinhead, or the triplet base within procentrioles and the proximal region of the parental centriole.
source: Within procentrioles and the proximal region of the parental centriole, it is possible that these four proteins help form the A-C linker, the pinhead, or the triplet base.
evidence: This is speculation about the structural role of the complex.

claim: Three of the proteins in the complex (TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1) had shared co-dependencies with A-C linker components using DepMap.
source: Recently, components of the A-C linker have been identified (Bournonville et al., 2024; Laporte et al., 2024), and three of the proteins in our complex (TEDC2, TUBD1, and TUBE1) had shared co-dependencies with A-C linker components using DepMap (Bournonville et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bournonville et al., 2024.

claim: It is not clear whether the loss of A-C linkers in mutant centrioles is due to a direct role of these proteins in forming A-C linkers or an indirect role of the triplet microtubules in stabilizing A-C linkers.
source: The A-C linker is lost from our mutant centrioles, but it is not clear whether this is because these proteins have a direct role in forming A-C linkers or whether this reflects an indirect role of the triplet microtubules in stabilizing A-C linkers.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism of A-C linker loss.

claim: It is possible that only some proteins of the complex, such as delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, form structural components of centrioles.
source: We note that it is also possible that only some proteins of the complex, such as delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, form structural components of centrioles, or that the complex may interact transiently with centrioles.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative models for how the complex functions.

claim: The complex may interact transiently with centrioles.
source: We note that it is also possible that only some proteins of the complex, such as delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, form structural components of centrioles, or that the complex may interact transiently with centrioles.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative models for how the complex functions.
